case_name: Anjani K. Verma v State of Bihar and Another
respondent:
State of Bihar and Another
Supreme Court of India

24 March 2004
Cr.A. No. 966 of 1998
The Order of the Court was as follows:
1.  This appeal is directed against the judgment of the High Court whereby petition filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the appellant for expunging the remarks against him as contained in the judgment of learned Sessions Judge dated 7-2-1998, was dismissed.
2.  At the outset, we may observe that a judicial officer who exceeds the limits of propriety and conduct and does not render justice in accordance with the facts of the case and the law, needs no protection from the superior courts. But, at the same time, while passing strictures against a member of the subordinate judiciary utmost care and caution is required to be taken, also having regard to the stress and conditions under which, by and large, the judicial officers have to render justice. statutes.act: Read With Section 34 Of The Indian Penal Code

facts: The Order of the Court was as follows: ...
A judicial officer who exceeds the limits of propriety and conduct and does not render justice in accordance with the facts of the case and the law, needs no protection from the superior courts.
... utmost care and caution is required to be taken, also having regard to the stress and conditions under which, by and large, the judicial officers have to render justice.

The appellant as a judicial officer (Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Dhanbad), by judgment dated 6-5-1997 trying a case under Section 498-A Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Sections 3/4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, acquitted the two accused who had been charged for the said offence giving them benefit of doubt.

The Sessions Judge, Dhanbad, trying altogether a different case for offences under Sections 364, 302 and Section 201 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, by judgment dated 7-2-1998 convicted one of the accused and acquitted the other.
It is a detailed judgment setting out the evidence in the case and recording reasons for the order of acquittal.

The Sessions Judge though observed that it was not the proper forum to make observations against the Magistrate, that is to say, the Sessions Judge was trying an altogether separate case and the Magistrate had decided an altogether separate case.
It does not appear that the evidence that had been led in the case decided by the appellant was before the Sessions, Judge in the case in which these strictures were passed.
Only a copy of the judgment was placed on the record of the sessions trial by the accused by way of defence.

In this view, conclusion was reached that the entire prosecution story of alleged torture and demand of dowry was surrounded with shadow of doubts, on account whereof the benefit of doubt was given to the accused.

Further, it appears that the observations in the impugned judgment of the High Court that no show-cause notice had been issued to the appellant, are also not correct, since, as abovenoticed, the show-cause notice dated 3-3-1998 had been issued.
A perusal of petition under Section 482 CrPC shows that the notice dated 3-3-1998 had been annexed thereto.
issues: What is the proper procedure for a superior court to follow when passing strictures against a member of the subordinate judiciary?
Can a Sessions Judge pass strictures against a Magistrate without record and evidence of the case?
Is it justified to attribute improper motive to a judicial officer based on his order of acquittal?
petitioner_arguments: The appellant argued that the strictures passed by the Sessions Judge were unjustified and that he had given benefit of doubt to the accused.
The appellant also argued that the Sessions Judge did not have record and evidence of the case before passing the strictures.
The appellant further argued that the High Court's decision to dismiss the petition was incorrect.
respondent_arguments: The respondent/defending party did not present any arguments in this judgment.
There are no specific arguments presented by the respondent in this judgment.
court_reasoning: The court observed that a judicial officer who exceeds the limits of propriety and conduct and does not render justice in accordance with the facts of the case and the law, needs no protection from the superior courts.
The court also noted that utmost care and caution is required to be taken when passing strictures against a member of the subordinate judiciary.
The court further observed that the Sessions Judge did not have record and evidence of the case before passing the strictures.
The court concluded that there was no justification for passing the strictures against the appellant.
holding: The appeal is accordingly allowed. The strictures passed against the appellant are expunged.
